notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on Hague Convention consent, ne exeat rights of custody, and autonomous Convention interpretation; outcome and ratio are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Hague Convention return: consent, ne exeat and rights of custody

statutes_considered.title: Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980

key_facts: A 10-year-old child was removed from New York to England by her mother in February 2003 despite court orders restricting removal from the state.
Johnson J found the father had signed a written consent note and held that removal was not wrongful; he also dismissed an inherent jurisdiction application.
The father appealed on consent, the interaction of consent with Articles 3 and 13, and whether he had rights of custody under New York law.
Handwriting experts disagreed on whether the father signed the consent document; no oral evidence was heard at first instance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted on notice from the father's unsuccessful Hague Convention and inherent jurisdiction applications for the child's return to the United States.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; child to be returned immediately to New York under Article 12; further orders as agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Consent is to be determined under Article 13(a), not Article 3; rights of custody under the Hague Convention receive an autonomous interpretation and a ne exeat clause in a New York custody order can constitute rights of custody even if US federal law does not; the mother failed to establish consent and the first-instance judge erred in preferring handwriting evidence without adequate reasons.
legal_issues: Whether the father consented to the child's removal
Whether consent negates wrongfulness under Article 3 or only engages Article 13 discretion
Whether rights of custody are determined by the law of habitual residence or by autonomous Convention meaning
Whether a ne exeat clause confers rights of custody for Convention purposes
linked_authorities: Re C (Abduction: Consent) [1996] 1 FLR 416
C v C (Abduction: Rights of Custody) [1989] 1 WLR 654
Re F (A Minor) (Abduction: Custody Rights Abroad) [1995] Fam 224
Re H (Abduction: Acquiescence) [1998] AC 72
English v Emery Reinbold & Strick Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 605

confidence.notes: Detailed full judgment with clear holdings on all three appeal issues. Inherent jurisdiction reasoning at first instance is secondary to the Hague Convention outcome.

notes: TCC judgment on dominant purpose and waiver of litigation privilege over the Pickavance audit report; findings on misleading representations are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Pickavance report disclosure: litigation privilege and estoppel
key_facts: LFEPA retained Roy Pickavance to investigate a fire house project that had overrun from about £7.6m and 12 months to about £14m over four years.
Halcrow, the project manager, cooperated in extensive interviews and document disclosure believing the work was a members' technical audit.
The Authority told Halcrow the dominant purpose was audit and public accountability; internally it sought evidence for contemplated claims.
Halcrow applied for specific disclosure of the Pickavance report and associated working documents; the Authority claimed litigation privilege.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for specific disclosure in TCC proceedings arising from LFEPA's claims against Halcrow over the Southwark training centre fire house project.
enrichment.outcome: Pickavance report ordered to be disclosed; question of disclosure of associated working documents left premature.
enrichment.ratio: The dominant purpose of the Pickavance report was project audit for elected members, not litigation; even if privilege were prima facie available, the Authority estopped itself by falsely representing the purpose to Halcrow, on which Halcrow relied in allowing employee interviews beyond contractual obligation.
legal_issues: Whether the Pickavance report attracted litigation privilege on dominant purpose
Whether privilege was lost by misleading Halcrow as to the purpose of the investigation
Whether disclosure of interview transcripts waived privilege in the report
Whether legal advice privilege could attach via Winyard Fearon's advice

London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority

notes: Maritime collision appeal with Elder Brethren advice; fault apportionment and Rule 9(d) analysis are well reasoned though includes procedural postscript on assessors.

enrichment.short_title: Suez Canal grounding: dredger and tanker fault apportionment

statutes_considered.title: International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (Collision Regulations)

key_facts: The laden chemical tanker BOW SPRING grounded outside the Suez Canal Northern By-pass Channel on 8 July 1999 after altering hard to starboard.
The dredger MANZANILLO II was returning from a spoil run on a south-westerly course at about 10 knots near the dredging zone.
The master beached the tanker fearing the dredger would cross the channel ahead; rudder and propeller damage followed.
David Steel J held the dredger 50% and the tanker 50% to blame; the dredger owners appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a collision action judgment apportioning blame for grounding and consequent damage in the Suez Canal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; 50/50 apportionment upheld; respondents' costs on the standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: The dredger was at fault for not making clear early that she would not cross the narrow channel and impede the draft-restricted tanker under Rule 9(d); that fault causally contributed to the master's over-reaction in leaving the channel, though reducing speed rather than beaching would have been appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether the MANZANILLO II was partly at fault for the grounding
Whether dredger fault was causative of the BOW SPRING leaving the channel
Whether equal apportionment was correct
Procedural fairness when nautical assessors' advice is not disclosed to parties before judgment
linked_authorities: The Pelopidas [1999] 2 Lloyd's Rep 675
The Sitarem [2001] 2 Lloyd's Rep 107
The Statue of Liberty [1971] 2 Lloyd's Rep 277
Kr Ma v Czech Republic (35376/97)

confidence.notes: Core fault and causation holdings are clear. Postscript on assessor procedure is obiter guidance, not part of the appeal disposition.

notes: Long planning s288 challenge on certificate of lawfulness for curtilage use; all four grounds dismissed with detailed Burdle analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Fernhill Cottage curtilage certificate of lawfulness challenge
key_facts: Miss Catherine Stewart sought a certificate of lawfulness for use of land (Area 2) beside Fernhill Cottage, Caudle Green, as residential curtilage including for a carer's mobile home.
The council granted a certificate for Area 1 and part of Area 2 (a 4m strip with septic tank) but refused the remainder (Area 2A).
Inspector Roberts allowed a limited appeal on appeal, certifying only the black-hatched strip for incidental domestic uses.
Historical evidence from 1948 onwards suggested Area 2 had been agricultural or casually used, not materially changed to domestic curtilage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to quash a planning inspector's decision and certificate of lawfulness following a partial success on a section 191/195 appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused; Secretary of State awarded costs summarily assessed at £4,074.
enrichment.ratio: The inspector was entitled on the evidence to treat Area 2A as a separate agricultural planning unit from Fernhill Cottage and Area 1; the claimant's use since 1992 was insufficient in nature and intensity for a material change of use, and disability does not alter the objective material-change-of-use test.
legal_issues: Whether Area 2A was a separate planning unit with established agricultural use
Whether the inspector erred in relying on Mr Gerald Stewart's unsigned proof on grazing
Whether a mobile home for a carer would be incidental to dwelling use
Whether a lesser intensity test applies where the landowner is disabled
linked_authorities: Burdle v Secretary of State for the Environment [1972] 1 WLR 1207
Ashbridge Investments Ltd v Minister of Housing and Local Government [1965] 1 WLR 1320
G Percy Trentham Ltd v Gloucestershire County Council [1966] 1 WLR 506
Bolton Metropolitan District Council v Secretary of State for the Environment [1995] 3 PLR 37
Whitehead v Secretary of State for the Environment [1992] JPL 561

confidence.notes: Four grounds fully reasoned. Paragraph 8 of the inspector's decision on mobile homes held obiter and to be disregarded in future.

notes: Insurance appeal on wear-and-tear exclusion after Hatfield; proximate cause analysis overturns Steel J on narrow ESR-by-ESR basis.

enrichment.short_title: Rail insurers' wear-and-tear exclusion after Hatfield ESRs
key_facts: After the Hatfield derailment on 17 October 2000, Railtrack imposed emergency speed restrictions at RCF/GCC sites across the network.
Five train operating companies claimed business interruption losses under the CGNU policy denial-of-access extension.
Steel J declared cover in principle for losses from ESRs between 17 and 31 October 2000 but held wear and tear was not a proximate cause.
Eagle Star (25% line) appealed only the wear-and-tear exclusion point; there was no appeal on whether each ESR was a separate occurrence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court declaration on construction of a rail business interruption policy following Hatfield-related speed restrictions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on wear-and-tear proximate cause; Jacob and Brooke LJJ agreed; prior declaration on cover otherwise unaffected by this point.
enrichment.ratio: Rolling contact fatigue was a proximate (or co-proximate) cause of each ESR-related loss because track wear and tear caused the restrictions to be imposed; the ESR was not merely the occasion for action, and the general wear-and-tear exclusion applied to the denial-of-access extension subject to all policy terms.
legal_issues: Whether RCF/wear and tear was the proximate cause of ESR-related business interruption losses
Whether the wear-and-tear exclusion applied to the denial-of-access extension
Whether each ESR or the Railtrack programme should be treated as the occurrence
Application of Wayne Tank proximate cause principles
linked_authorities: Wayne Tank and Pump Co Ltd v Employers Liability Assurance Corporation Ltd [1974] 1 QB 57
Leyland Shipping Co Ltd v Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd [1918] AC 350
The Miss Jay Jay [1987] 1 Lloyd's Rep 32
Gray v Barr [1971] QB 554

confidence.notes: Focused appeal on one exclusion issue; judge's non-appealed findings on occurrences and cover scope noted in judgment.

notes: Commercial Court section 68 application on LMAA small claims confidential reasons; allows reliance on reasons but dismisses on merits.

enrichment.short_title: Confidential arbitration reasons and section 68 challenge
key_facts: Buyers and sellers disputed liability under Norwegian Saleform clause 19 after an underwater inspection found excessive rudder pintle clearance on the vessel Easy Rider.
Parties agreed US$50,000 escrow and referred the dispute to LMAA small claims arbitration; Anthony Scott issued an unreasoned award with separate confidential reasons.
The arbitrator awarded US$6,094 to buyers based on the sellers' repair quotation; buyers sought remission under section 68.
Buyers argued unfair procedure and disregard of their shipyard quotation; sellers argued confidential reasons could not be used.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 68 application to remit or set aside an LMAA small claims arbitration award on serious irregularity grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; court permitted buyers to rely on confidential reasons but found no serious irregularity on either ground.
enrichment.ratio: Parties may contract not to use confidential reasons in challenge proceedings, but the court may admit them where section 68 alleges serious irregularity causing substantial injustice and they are the only evidence of how the arbitrator decided; here the arbitrator's construction of clause 19 and damages assessment involved no such irregularity.
legal_issues: Whether confidential LMAA reasons may be relied on in section 68 proceedings
Whether the arbitrator decided the case on an issue not fairly raised
Whether the arbitrator wrongly ignored the buyers' repair quotation
Interaction of party autonomy, finality, and section 68 'long stop' jurisdiction

Atlantic Lines and Navigation Co Inc v Italmare SpA (The Apollon) [1985] 1 Lloyd's Rep 597
Bulfracht (Cyprus) Ltd v Boneset Shipping Co Ltd (The Pamphilos) [2002] 2 Lloyd's Rep 681

confidence.notes: Detailed review of confidential-reasons authorities and clear dismissal on both section 68 grounds.

notes: Planning committee vote miscount JR; Forbes J overturned on procedural fairness when objectors' recount request not referred to chair.

enrichment.short_title: Planning committee vote miscount judicial review
key_facts: Cannock Chase Planning Control Committee recorded a 7-6 vote approving amended plans for development neighbouring the Tromans' property on 2 April 2003.
Objectors counted 7-6 against approval, including dispute over whether Councillor Boyle voted after re-entering the chamber.
Mrs Hill and the Tromans immediately raised a miscount with officers; the planning head said it was too late to revisit during the meeting.
The chair and planning officer maintained a correct 7-6 approval count verified by legal services.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of judicial review of planning permission granted after a disputed committee vote; appeal limited to the vote-count ground.
enrichment.ratio: Where objectors bona fide and promptly disputed a close committee vote, fairness required the query to be put to the chair or committee for a decision on verification; failure to do so was procedural unfairness even absent bad faith in the original count.
legal_issues: Duty of fairness when a vote count is disputed at a planning committee meeting
Whether refusal to recount was Wednesbury unreasonable
Applicability of St Pancras Vestrymen principles without statutory voting rules
Whether the committee remained able to verify votes before formal permission issued
linked_authorities: R v Commissioner of Racial Equality ex parte Hillingdon LBC [1982] AC 779
R v The Vestrymen and Churchwardens of St Pancras Middlesex (1839) 11 Ad & El 15

confidence.notes: Single-issue appeal with clear unfairness finding. Factual dispute on count unresolved but procedural defect sufficient for relief.

notes: Consented civil proceedings order under section 42; unlimited order with carve-out for Tennal group litigation application.

enrichment.short_title: Unlimited civil proceedings order against vexatious litigant
key_facts: The Attorney General applied for a civil proceedings order against Paul Benton under section 42; Benton consented.
Between April 2001 and June 2003 Benton issued at least 32 claims, many struck out as abusive or without reasonable grounds, including actions against judges and the Prime Minister.
Psychiatric evidence linked habitual litigation to delusional mental illness; medication compliance improved from late 2003.
Parties disputed whether a time-limited order was appropriate and whether Benton could join the Tennal Group Litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application for a civil proceedings order under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981, heard by a Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Unlimited civil proceedings order made; permission granted for Benton to apply to join Tennal Group Litigation (BM 303969 and BM 117029) excluded from the order.
enrichment.ratio: Persistent habitual vexatious litigation over 26 months justified an indefinite civil proceedings order where psychiatric evidence gave no rational basis to expect future abatement; a limited order was inappropriate given the wide range of defendants and subjects pursued.
legal_issues: Whether statutory preconditions for a section 42 order were satisfied
Whether the order should be time-limited or indefinite
Whether the Tennal Group Litigation claim should be excluded or subject to leave to apply to join
linked_authorities: Attorney General v Price (9 March 1997, unreported)
Attorney General v Yeo (8 December 1999, unreported)

confidence.notes: Consent simplified the hearing but court still satisfied itself on statutory conditions and discretion. Prior litigation chronology summarised not fully reviewed.

notes: Bond trustee indemnity appeal; Court overturns VC on wrongful acceleration damages but declines immediate acceleration declaration pending Event of Default determination.

enrichment.short_title: Bond trustee indemnity and ineffective acceleration notice
key_facts: Concord Trust held about 10% of €510m Elektrim bonds guaranteed by Elektrim and secured by a pledge over ET shares holding PTC telecom interests.
Bondholders certified an Event of Default after Elektrim suspended the bondholders' board nominee; more than 30% requested acceleration under Condition 12.
Law Debenture refused Concord's indemnity as insufficient given feared €876m–€1bn Elektrim claim for wrongful acceleration.
The Vice-Chancellor dismissed Concord's Part 8 claim for a declaration obliging immediate acceleration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Part 8 declaration refusing to order the bond trustee to accelerate repayment without a bank-grade indemnity.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; VC order set aside; no immediate acceleration declaration; trustee to commence urgent proceedings to determine whether an Event of Default occurred, subject to satisfactory indemnity for costs.
enrichment.ratio: A Condition 12 acceleration notice given when no Event of Default has occurred is contractually ineffective and not a breach of contract; the trustee therefore unreasonably demanded a €1bn indemnity based on a fanciful wrongful-acceleration damages scenario, but bondholders are not entitled to a declaration forcing acceleration while Elektrim disputes that an Event of Default occurred.
legal_issues: Whether an ineffective acceleration notice constitutes breach of contract by the trustee
What indemnity the trustee may require before accelerating under Condition 12
Whether Wednesbury unreasonableness or worst-case scenario governs review of trustee satisfaction
Whether Elektrim could recover substantial damages for economic impairment triggered by acceleration
linked_authorities: Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223
Borealis AB v Stargas Ltd [2002] AC 205
Re H (Abduction: Acquiescence) [1998] AC 72

confidence.notes: Detailed reasoning on ineffective notice and indemnity. Remedial path forward stated in general terms pending further case management.
